newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrican amnesty bid may shed light on Hani murder.
newsitem.headline: SAfrican amnesty bid may shed light on Hani murder.

text.p: South Africa's truth commission on Monday began considering amnesty for the murderers of Communist Party leader Chris Hani, whose 1993 death nearly wrecked the transition from apartheid.

Polish-born Janusz Walus, the assassin, and right-wing politician Clive Derby-Lewis, who furnished the gun, are seeking amnesty for a deed they will speak publicly about for the first time at the Pretoria hearing.
But the family of Hani, who was second only to President Nelson Mandela as a popular hero, fiercely opposes freedom for the unusual pair whose 1993 death sentences were commuted to life in prison.
The family's lawyer, George Bizos, asked to be allowed to produce police statements by the two men and by Derby-Lewis' wife Gaye, a co-defendant, to prove they had not told the full story.
"Mrs Derby-Lewis was acquitted of murder. Nothing can happen to her whatever she may have said," said Bizos, who defended Mandela in a 1964 trial where he was jailed for life.

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC), set up by Mandela to expose and heal apartheid-era crimes, has the power to grant amnesty to applicants who tell all and who can prove their crimes had political motives.
Lawyers for Walus and Derby-Lewis said their statements were made involuntarily and under duress under apartheid security laws that permitted detention without trial.
Hani's death on April 10, Easter Saturday, hit South Africa like an earthquake during one of the hardest periods of the long negotiations that ended in free elections a year later.

"Derby-Lewis must serve life" and "You are murderers" read placards held by Hani supporters who sang at breaks in the hearing at Pretoria's forbidding City Hall, decorated with romanticised paintings showing moments in Afrikaner history.
Hani, who many believed could have been the next president after Mandela, led the African National Congress' armed wing in exile but by 1993 was committed to a negotiated settlement.
Walus, a fierce anti-communist who left martial-law Poland for South Africa in 1981, shot Hani four times outside his home in a middle-class suburb east of Johannesburg.
A white neighbour, Rheta Harmse, memorised his number plate and alerted police who arrested him 10 minutes later.
The evidence led to Derby-Lewis, a former member of the all-white parliament for the far-right Conservative Party on whose behalf he claims the assassination was carried out.
"Here is not a question of guilt or innocence. The committee is dealing with two convicted murderers," Bizos told the hearing.
"The issue is have they made full disclosure?
"And are they telling the truth when they contend they acted on behalf of the Conservative Party?"
In his amnesty application Walus said he had "vowed to to something to try and stop the handover to communist rule", fearing Hani would recreate a Soviet-style state.
The two murderers are expected to testify at the two-week-long hearing, but it is not clear when they will take the stand or when the commission might announce a ruling on their application.

The Pretoria hearing, coming days after the commission granted amnesty to notorious state hit-squad killer Dirk Coetzee, brought grey-haired and grey-suited followers of Derby-Lewis together with Hani's wife and daughter.
A year after Hani's death, South Africans voted in all-race elections. The much-feared bloody civil war had been avoided.
Mandela had helped defuse one of the tensest moments with a presidential-style televised appeal to the nation for calm after Hani's killing.
Referring to Walus and the neighbour who caught him, he repeated a favourite message -- that there were good and bad in every race.
"A white man, full of prejudice and hate, came to our country and committed a deed so foul that our whole nation now teeters on the brink of disaster," Mandela said.
"But a white woman, of Afrikaner origin, risked her life so that we may know, and bring to justice, the assassin."
Officials said lawyers would to continue their presentations to the hearing on Tuesday.
